title: Suspense Mechanism: Promise Throwing, Boundary Catches & Resolution

progressiveExplaining.eli5: When a worker in a factory runs out of raw materials, they hit a pause button (throw a Promise). The supervisor in that room (the `<Suspense>` boundary) immediately puts up a 'Work in Progress' sign (the fallback). When the supply truck arrives with the materials, the supervisor tears down the sign and tells the worker to pick up where they paused.
progressiveExplaining.junior: React `<Suspense fallback={<Loading />}>` lets components pause rendering while waiting for asynchronous operations. When an async resource (like a Promise via React 19 `use()`, `React.lazy()`, or a data library like Relay) is not ready, the component literally throws the pending Promise. The nearest `<Suspense>` boundary catches the thrown promise, displays the fallback, attaches a listener to the promise, and re-renders the component once the promise resolves.
progressiveExplaining.senior: Architecturally, Suspense repurposes JavaScript's `throw` mechanism as an algebraic effect for control flow. In the Render Phase, when a fiber throws a `Thenable`, the work loop intercepts it in `handleThrow()`. React marks the nearest parent Suspense fiber with the `DidCapture` flag, unwinds the work-in-progress stack, mounts the fallback UI in the current commit, and registers a resolution callback (`ping`) on the thrown promise. When the promise fulfills, React schedules a retry render on the suspended lane.
progressiveExplaining.underTheHood: In `renderRootConcurrent`, if a fiber throws a Promise, React executes `throwAndUnwindWorkLoop`. It searches up the `return` pointer chain for a `SuspenseComponent` fiber. Once found, it creates an alternate branch rendering the `fallback` prop. React attaches `.then(pingListener, pingListener)` to the thrown Promise. When the promise resolves, `pingListener` executes `retryTimedOutBoundary` or `pingSuspendedRoot`, dispatching a scheduler task to re-render the suspended subtree with the now-fulfilled data.

interviewGotchas.question: What happens if a component suspended inside `<Suspense>` throws a rejected Promise?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: Tests your understanding of the relationship between Suspense and Error Boundaries.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: When a Promise rejects, the nearest `<Suspense>` boundary cannot resolve it. React treats the rejected promise as a runtime execution error and bubbles the rejection up the tree until it is caught by the nearest **`<ErrorBoundary>`**. If no Error Boundary exists, the application crashes.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: Suspense boundaries only catch *pending* promises to show fallback loading UI; they do *not* catch rejected promises or errors. Always pair `<Suspense>` with an `<ErrorBoundary>`.

interviewGotchas.question: Why does React discard and restart rendering from scratch when a suspended component resolves?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: Checks knowledge of React's pure render phase contract during Suspense retries.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: Because state or context could have changed while the promise was pending in the background, React cannot simply resume from the middle of the suspended component. When the promise resolves (`ping`), React restarts the render pass for that subtree from the Suspense boundary downwards to guarantee complete state consistency across the new render cycle.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: Components suspended under Suspense must remain pure and free from render-phase side effects, as they may be evaluated multiple times before committing.
